output_raw: {"text":"I still remember my first day at university very clearly because it was a mix of excitement and nervousness that I had never felt before. I had imagined the campus would be huge and the classes would be more interesting than any high school subject, so I expected to meet a lot of friendly people and to learn a lot of new things very quickly. When I arrived early in the morning, the big stone building with the blue glass windows looked even more impressive than the pictures on the brochure, and I felt a little bit lost among the crowd of students. I met a senior named Linh who was from the same hometown as me, and she introduced me to a group of freshmen who were also looking for friends. We chatted about our subjects, and I discovered that most of them were studying engineering like me, which made me feel less alone. After the orientation lecture, we were taken on a campus tour where we visited the library, the sports complex and the cafeteria. I was most nervous than I had expected during the tour because I was afraid I would get lost, but the guide was very helpful and the group was supportive. Later, we had a short ice‑breaker activity where we had to share one interesting fact about ourselves, and I said that I could play the guitar, which surprised some of the others. By the end of the day I felt that I should could manage my schedule better and that I would be able to adapt to university life. This whole experience boosted my confidence a lot; I left the campus feeling more confident than I ever felt before, and it gave me the courage to join clubs and take part in class discussions from the very next week."}

output_raw: {"text":"I’d like to talk about a challenging project I worked on during my final year of high school, it was a science fair exhibition where our team had to design a simple water purification system using locally available materials. The main goal of the project was to create a device that could reduce contaminants in river water to a level safe for drinking, and we also wanted to present the whole process in a clear and engaging way for the judges and other students. At first, I thought it would be easy because we had some basic knowledge about filtration, but soon we faced several obstacles. One big problem was that the budget was very limited, so we could not buy commercial filters and we had to improvise with sand, charcoal and some plastic bottles. Another difficulty was that the chemistry teacher, who was supposed to guide us, was away for a few weeks, so we had to figure out the right chemical reactions on our own. If I would have known how important the teacher’s input was, I might have planned a backup plan earlier. Also, we ran into time constraints because the school schedule changed and we lost a week of lab access, which meant we had to work late evenings at home. During the testing phase, the prototype kept leaking, and I think we tried different sealing methods but none of them worked at first. Eventually, we discovered that using a rubber gasket from an old bike tire solved the leakage problem. The outcome was that we managed to produce a functional purifier that could lower turbidity by about seventy percent, and we won the second prize at the fair. After the presentation, I felt a mixture of relief and pride. I was relieved because all the hard work finally paid off, and I was proud because I learned how to solve problems creatively and work as a team under pressure. Looking back, the experience also taught me that planning for unexpected issues and asking for help early can make a big difference in any project."}

output_raw: {"text":"Well, I would like to talk about the Lunar New Year festival, which is my favourite seasonal celebration every year. It usually falls in late January or early February, so it is a winter festival for us, although the weather is starting to get warmer. The most important tradition is the family reunion dinner, which we have on the eve of the new year at home. We clean the house completely before that day, because it is believed that cleaning removes the bad luck from the previous year. Then we decorate the living room with red lanterns and couplets, and we put a special cake on the table for the ancestors. Another tradition is the giving of lucky money, called \"li xi\", which we give to children and also to younger relatives, and we do it in the morning after the first sunrise of the new year. We also go to the temple for a prayer, where we light incense and offer fruits on the altar, and we stay there for about half an hour. I usually celebrate with my parents, my wife and my two children, and sometimes my older brother comes from the city to join us. My friends also come over to share some traditional foods, such as spring rolls and sticky rice cakes. The festival means a lot to me because it is not only about having fun, it is about respecting our culture and keeping the family bond strong. It reminds me of my childhood when I used to watch my grandparents preparing the food and telling stories about the ancient customs. In a way, celebrating Lunar New Year each year gives me a sense of continuity and hope for the future, and it also helps me to stay connected with my roots while living in a modern city."}

input._prior_text:
To be honest, I have a strong preference for physical books. There is something quite tactile about turning the pages and feeling the weight of the volume in my hands that simply cannot be replicated on a screen. Digital formats are certainly more convenient for travel, but I find that I focus better when I am not constantly distracted by notifications popping up on my phone. I tend to gravitate towards literary fiction and non-fiction pieces about psychology. I find it fascinating to explore the complexities of human behavior and see how different authors interpret social dynamics. Lately, I have been really into biographies of successful entrepreneurs because they often contain practical insights that I can apply to my own career development and daily life situations. It was actually just a few days ago. I spent a rainy Sunday afternoon finishing a novel called The Silent Echo. It was a really engaging story about a family dealing with a mysterious inheritance. I barely noticed the time flying by, which is a great sign. I usually only get around to reading for pleasure when I have a bit of free time. Definitely during holidays. When I am working full-time, my evenings are usually consumed by rest and social commitments, so I rarely have the mental energy to sit down with a new book. However, during vacation, I can dedicate entire mornings to reading without feeling rushed. It is one of the few times of year when I can truly disconnect from my work responsibilities. I think it's Instagram, because I use it for both staying in touch with friends and following news. I usually open it first thing in the morning, and then again during lunch break, so I end up checking it maybe five or six times a day, especially when there are new stories or live videos. On a typical weekday I would say I spend around three to four hours in front of screen, including work, social media and some videos. I try to limit it after work, but sometimes I end up watching series on Netflix because I want to relax, so total can reach close to five hours sometimes. I really enjoy playing role‑playing games, especially ones with open worlds where I can explore and complete quests. I like the freedom to make choices, and the stories are usually very engaging. When I have free time I often pick up a game like "Elder Scrolls" because it lets me get lost in fantasy setting for hours. Yes, I actually stopped using a photo‑editing app that I loved a lot. It was great for adding filters, but after a while the updates became too frequent and it started using a lot of battery, so I decided to switch to another one that is more stable and doesn't require so many permissions. I’d like to talk about a gift that I received a few years ago and still keep it close to my heart. It was given to me by my older sister, Linh, on the day I graduated from university. She handed me a small wooden box, about the size of a paperback book, with intricate carvings of lotus flowers and swirling patterns on its lid. Inside, there was a leather‑bound journal, its pages slightly yellowed, and a silver pen that felt surprisingly heavy when I held it. I remember the moment vividly because the ceremony was held in a quiet garden, and after everyone had taken photos, Linh pulled me aside and said, "I hope you write down all your dreams in this," with a smile that made me feel both proud and a little nervous about future.

What makes this gift so special isn’t just its appearance but the meaning behind it. The wooden box itself is handcrafted by a local artisan in my hometown, and each time I look at the lotus carvings, I think of my family’s roots and the calmness that lotus represents in Vietnamese culture. The journal, on the other hand, became a place where I recorded my first job experiences, travel plans, and even some poetry I wrote during late nights. Even though I’ve moved to a new city for work, I still keep the box on my desk, and the pen sits right next to my laptop, reminding me of the support that Linh gave me.

It remains important because it symbolizes a turning point in my life – the transition from student to professional – and it carries the love and encouragement of my sister. Whenever I feel stressed or uncertain, I open the journal, read the first entry I wrote on graduation day, and it instantly lifts my spirits, making me feel connected to my past and motivated for future challenges.

input._prior_text: Well, I usually make fried rice with shrimp and vegetables, because it's quick and everyone in my family likes it. I also add some soy sauce and a bit of chili, makes it tasty. Sometimes I use chicken instead of shrimp, when I have leftovers from last night, it's still delicious and satisfying. I avoid eating liver, because the smell and texture not pleasant for me. My mother always cooked it when I was little, but I never liked the strong iron taste. Also, I think it's heavy on the stomach, sometimes makes me feel uneasy after a big meal, so I just stay away from it. I try to go to the market twice a week, usually on Saturday and Wednesday. That way I can get fresh vegetables and meat, and also check for any promotions. If I run out of something in between, I might stop by a small convenience store, but I prefer the larger supermarket for most of my shopping. I would love to learn how to cook Italian food, especially homemade pasta and sauce. The flavors sound amazing, and I think it would be fun to experiment with fresh tomatoes, basil, and cheese. Also, making pizza from scratch seems challenging but exciting, so I hope to take a cooking class soon. I genuinely believe that handmade items carry the most weight because the creator puts actual time and emotion into the process. Unlike mass-produced goods, a hand-knitted scarf or a custom-written letter shows that you truly understand the recipient's personality. It demonstrates effort rather than just spending money, which makes the gesture feel much more personal and meaningful to me. Yes, last Christmas I bought a fancy watch for my uncle. He was quite polite at first, but I noticed he never wore it once. Later, my aunt told me he found the style too flashy for his daily routine. I felt a bit embarrassed then. Maybe I should have asked him about his preferences earlier to avoid such awkward situation in the future. I would definitely prefer a physical object. Cash feels too transactional and cold, like a business payment rather than a celebration of our relationship. A tangible item creates a lasting memory that I can hold and look at later. It serves as a constant reminder of the person who gave it, which cash simply cannot do for me emotionally. I usually start shopping about two weeks before any major holiday. Buying early helps me avoid the intense crowds and the risk of popular items selling out completely. It also gives me enough time to wrap things carefully and ensure everything arrives safely. Rushing at the last minute always makes the process stressful and less enjoyable for me personally. Well, I’d like to talk about a day I spent away from home last summer, when I went to a coastal town called Thuy Hai, not far from my city. It was a Saturday, and I decided to take a short trip with two of my friends, Linh and Quang, because we all felt the need to escape the usual routine and get some fresh sea air. We left early in the morning, around seven, catching a train that runs directly to the town’s main station. The journey itself was pretty comfortable, the scenery changed from the busy streets of Hanoi to green rice fields and finally to the sparkling coastline, which made me feel excited even before we arrived. Once we got there, the first thing we did was to check into a small guesthouse near the beach, a place recommended by a local travel blog I read last month. The room was simple but clean, with a balcony that faced the sea, so we could hear the waves even while we were unpacking our bags. After freshening up, we headed straight to the beach. We walked along the sand, collected shells, and tried a bit of surfing, although none of us had any experience before, so we fell many times, but it was really fun. Later, we rented bicycles and rode around the town, stopping at a market where we tried some local street food – grilled fish, mango sticky rice, and a very spicy noodle soup that made my eyes water, but I loved the flavors. In the afternoon, we visited a small museum that displayed the history of the fishing community, and a guide explained how the locals have been living off the sea for generations. The whole day was full of activities, from relaxing on the beach, exploring the town, to learning about its culture. By the evening, we sat at a seaside café, watching the sunset, and we talked about our plans for the future, feeling a mixture of happiness and a little bit of melancholy because we knew we had to go back to our daily lives soon. When we finally returned home late at night, I felt exhausted but also refreshed, like a battery had been recharged, and I realized how important it is to take a break and spend quality time with friends away from the usual environment.

Examiner: Do you prefer starting your day with exercise or a meal?
Candidate: I like meal. I eat meal. I do not exercise in the morning.
Examiner: How do you typically spend your lunch break at work or school?
Candidate: I go to eat. I eat rice. I eat fast. I go back.
Examiner: What is the last thing you do before going to bed?
Candidate: I check phone. I read news. I put phone down. I sleep.
Examiner: Do you often change your daily schedule when the weekend arrives?
Candidate: Yes, I change. I sleep late. I sleep long. I watch TV.
Examiner: Is the area where you live a busy or quiet place?
Candidate: The area is very busy, very busy, the traffic is always loud.
Examiner: Do you prefer living in a city center or the suburbs?
Candidate: I prefer the suburbs because it is quiet, quiet and cheaper than city.
Examiner: How do you usually travel to your favorite local spots?
Candidate: I usually go by motorbike to the park, I take a motorbike.
Examiner: Do you think your neighborhood has changed much in recent years?
Candidate: My neighbourhood has changed a lot, it was quiet then now it is more noisy.
Examiner: Describe a gift that you received which you still treasure. You should say: who gave it to you; what the item looks like; when you received it; and explain why it remains so important to you.
Candidate: So, I will talk about a gift. It is a small watch. My mother gave it to me. This watch is very old. It has a brown leather strap. The face is white with black numbers. It is a little broken, the glass is scratched. I received it on my birthday, I think it was when I was eight years old. I was very young, I remember the box was red. Why it is important? It is not about the money. It is about the love. My mother is very sick now, she is in hospital. So, I look at the watch, I feel the memory. It is my treasure.
Examiner: You mentioned the watch has a brown leather strap. Do you think material quality matters more than the sentiment behind a gift?
Candidate: Yes, yes, material is important. Brown leather is nice. But love is more. Love is big.
Examiner: You said your mother is very sick now. How does a physical object like a watch help people cope with loss?
Candidate: I look at watch. I feel sad. But also happy. It is my mother. It is in my hand.
Examiner: Earlier, you described the area as very busy and noisy. Do you think noise affects how we value quiet treasures?
Candidate: Noise is bad. I want quiet. Watch is quiet. It is small. It is peaceful. I like it.
Examiner: You mentioned the watch is a little broken. Should we repair old gifts or keep them as they are?
Candidate: No repair. Keep it. Broken is okay. It is old. It is real. I do not want new one.
Examiner: You said you prefer the suburbs because they are quiet. Do you think a calm environment helps people appreciate personal mementos better?
Candidate: Yes, quiet place is good. I think about watch. City is too loud. I cannot remember. Suburbs are better.

Candidate: I… I think I check Facebook most, because I have many friends there and I usually check it in the morning.
Examiner: What type of video game would you enjoy playing for fun?
Candidate: I like playing adventure games, like the one that I have played last week, it was very exciting and I wanted to try more.
Examiner: Have you ever stopped using an app you previously loved?
Candidate: Yes, I stopped using Instagram because I felt it was wasting my time, I have used it a lot before but I quit.
Examiner: Do you think technology makes leisure activities more or less enjoyable?
Candidate: I think technology makes them more enjoyable, because it gives us more options, but sometimes it also distracts us from real life.
Examiner: Describe a place in your city where you can relax. You should say: where the place is located; what it looks like inside; how you usually get there; and explain why you enjoy spending time there.
Candidate: I want to talk about a small park in my city. It is located near the center, but not too crowded. When I go there, I feel very calm. The park looks like a normal place with green trees and some benches. Inside, there is a small fountain and many flowers. I usually get there by bike because it is only five minutes away. I enjoy spending time there because I can breathe fresh air and escape from noise. Last week, I had a bad day at work, and I went to the park. I sat on a bench and watched people walking. It was very relaxing. I have been going there for two years, and I still like it very much. Sometimes I bring a book and read for one hour. It is my favorite place to relax in the city.
Examiner: In your description, you mentioned the park is not too crowded. Do you think public spaces are becoming less popular in your city?
Candidate: Yes, I think so. People are more busy now. They have been working long hours, so they do not have time to go outside. Maybe technology make them stay home more.
Examiner: You said you brought a book and read for one hour. Is reading alone a common way for people to relax today?
Candidate: I think yes, but not many people do it. I have read a book last week, it was very good. My friend, he prefer to play games on his phone instead of reading.
Examiner: You mentioned watching people walking while you sat on a bench. How important is it to observe others for mental health?
Candidate: It is quite important, I think. When I watched people, I felt calm. It helps me forget my stress. I have never tried meditation, but watching people feels similar for me.
Examiner: You said you want to add more benches and lighting to the park. Should local governments spend money on improving public parks?
Candidate: Definitely, yes. The government should do it. Parks are needed for our health. If it is dark at night, people feel scared. It has been a problem for a long time.
Examiner: You described the park as a place to escape from noise. Does living in a quiet suburb change how people interact with their neighbors?
Candidate: Maybe it does. In my suburb, it is more green and quiet. I do not know my neighbors very well. I have moved there last year, and I still feel a bit shy.

Candidate: Yes, I stopped using a photo editing app that I loved, because it became too expensive and the new updates were not useful, so I switched to a free alternative, although I miss some of the original features that were very helpful.
Examiner: Describe a mobile application that helps you in your daily life. You should say: what the app does for you; how often you use it; when you first installed it; and explain why you find it so useful.
Candidate: I would like to talk about a mobile application that I use almost every day, it is called TaskFlow and it basically helps me organise my schedule and keep track of my habits. I first installed it about two years ago when a friend recommended it because I was struggling to remember my appointments and I needed a tool that could send me reminders. Since then I use it at least three times a day, in the morning I check the tasks for the day, during lunch I update the progress of my fitness goals and in the evening I plan the next day’s activities. The app has a calendar view, a habit tracker and a note section, and the most useful feature is the smart notification system that can suggest the best time to do something based on my previous patterns, so I never forget to drink water or to call my parents. I think it is so helpful because it saves me a lot of time that I would otherwise spent searching for information or writing things down on paper, and it also gives me a sense of control over my life. If I could not rely on TaskFlow I would probably feel more stressed and disorganised, and I would be more likely to miss important deadlines, which would affect my work and personal life.
Examiner: You mentioned that TaskFlow gives you a sense of control over your life. Do you think technology generally makes people more organized or more distracted?
Candidate: I think it depends on how you use it. For me, it makes things more organized because I can see my daily plan clearly. However, if people check their phones too often, they might become more distracted than before. The app has a smart notification system, but I sometimes feel that too many alerts are noisy, so I would need to turn some of them off to stay focused on my work and personal tasks.
Examiner: You said you were struggling to remember appointments before using the app. How might this need for organization have been different when you were a child?
Candidate: When I was a child, I did not have so many complex schedules. My parents usually told me what to do, so I did not need to manage my time by myself. Now, as an adult, I have to handle many responsibilities, like work meetings and fitness goals. If I did not have a digital tool, I might forget important things, which would cause more stress for me and my family.
Examiner: You noted that you trust fresh produce at local shops more than online shopping. Do you believe this preference for tangible goods will change in the future?
Candidate: I think it might change because technology is improving very fast. In the future, online shops might use better quality control, so customers can trust the products more. However, I still like the experience of touching and smelling fruits myself. So, I suppose many people will keep this habit, even if they buy other things online. It is a mix of convenience and personal trust.
Examiner: You mentioned that you would feel stressed without the app. How do you think society will react if people become too dependent on such digital tools?
Candidate: I think society might face problems if people forget how to organize themselves without help. If we always rely on notifications, we might lose our own mental focus and memory skills. It is important to balance technology with our own abilities. I would try to remember things naturally, but I know it is hard when our lives are so busy and fast-paced nowadays.
Examiner: You said the app helps you track habits. Do you think it is better to have external rewards for good habits or to rely on internal motivation?
Candidate: I believe both are useful. External rewards, like seeing a green checkmark in the app, give me a quick satisfaction. But internal motivation is more important in the long run. If I only did things for the app, I might stop when I delete it. So, I try to remember why I exercise or drink water, to keep my health goals alive in my mind every single day.

input.text:
Examiner: What was the best present you received in the past year?
Candidate: The best present I got last year was a handmade guitar that my uncle made for me, because I love music and it sounds better than any cheap one I had before, and I use it every day when I practice.
Examiner: Have you ever given a gift that someone did not like?
Candidate: Yes, I once gave my friend a book about cooking, but she does not like cooking at all, so she said the gift was not useful for her and she prefer something more related to her hobby, like a sketch pad.
Examiner: Would you prefer a cash gift or a physical object?
Candidate: I think I would rather receive a physical object, because I enjoy having something I can see and touch, and a cash gift sometimes feels less personal than a thoughtful item that reminds me of the person who gave it.
Examiner: When is the best time of year to buy presents for family?
Candidate: In my opinion, the best time to buy presents for family is during the holiday season, especially around Christmas, because stores have many discounts and everyone is in a good mood, which makes choosing gifts easier and more enjoyable.
Examiner: What time do you usually wake up on weekdays?
Candidate: I typically wake up at six thirty every morning. My alarm is set for six, but I often snooze it twice. It is my hardest time of the day because I am so sleepy. However, I get up eventually because I must attend my classes at eight.
Examiner: Do you prefer starting your day with exercise or a meal?
Candidate: I definitely prefer eating breakfast first. It gives me energy for the day. I think exercise is better later, when my body is warm. If I run in the morning, I feel too tired to study. So, I always have some rice and tea before I start any physical activity.
Examiner: How do you typically spend your lunch break at work or school?
Candidate: Usually, I eat with my friends in the canteen. We talk about funny things that happens in class. It is a good way to relax. Sometimes, I just read a book alone because I need quiet time. I do not like crowded places when I am trying to rest my mind.
Examiner: What is the last thing you do before going to bed?
Candidate: The final thing I do is check my phone. I look at social media for about twenty minutes. It helps me unwind after a busy day. My sister says I should stop because the light is bad for my eyes, but I find it very comfortable and relaxing.
Examiner: Describe a place in your city where you can relax. You should say: where the place is located; what it looks like inside; how you usually get there; and explain why you enjoy spending time there.
Candidate: I would like to talk about a little garden that is near my university campus, and it is my favourite place to relax after classes. The garden is located behind the library, just next to the main road, and you can see it from the bus stop when you are heading to the lecture halls. Inside, the garden looks very peaceful, there are many kinds of trees, some of them are taller than the others, and there are also a small pond with lily pads and some colourful fish swimming around. The pathways are made of stone and they wind around the flower beds, which are full of roses, lavender and a few exotic plants that the horticulture club planted last year. I usually get there by walking from my dormitory, which is about ten minutes away, or sometimes I ride my bicycle if the weather is nice. The route is quite simple, I just turn left at the cafeteria, then go straight until I see the big oak tree, and the garden is right beside it. I enjoy spending time there because it feels much calmer than the noisy streets outside, and the fresh air there helps me to clear my mind before I study for exams. Also, I like to sit on one of the benches and read a book, because the environment is more relaxing than my room where there are many distractions.
Examiner: You mentioned that the garden is quieter than the streets. Do you think cities should have more green spaces for people to relax in?
Candidate: Yes, I strongly agree. A city without enough parks feels like a concrete box. People who live in apartments need a place where they can breathe fresh air and escape the noise. I think local governments should invest in more small gardens because it helps the mental health of residents, and it makes the urban environment more beautiful and livable for everyone.
Examiner: You said you ride your bicycle if the weather is nice. How has the rise of electric bikes and scooters changed the way people move around your city?
Candidate: It has changed a lot. Many students now prefer electric scooters because they are faster than walking and cheaper than taxis. However, I find that the roads are becoming more crowded and dangerous. There are too many people riding on sidewalks, which makes it hard for pedestrians. So, while it is convenient, I think it creates more problems for city planning and safety.
Examiner: Earlier, you mentioned reading a book on a bench to clear your mind. Do you think digital devices have made it harder for young people to find true relaxation?
Candidate: I think so. We are always checking our phones, so it is difficult to just sit quietly. The notifications from social media keep interrupting our focus. I remember when I read a physical book, I felt much more calm than when I use my tablet. Maybe we need to disconnect more often to really relax our minds and stop feeling so stressed out by technology.
Examiner: You described the lily pads and colourful fish in the pond. Do you believe that local wildlife is an important part of the identity of a city's natural areas?
Candidate: Absolutely. If you remove the fish and the birds, the garden just looks like a decoration. The animals give life to the space. I think a place where wildlife can thrive is more interesting than a manicured lawn. It shows that nature is still present in the city, and it helps young people connect with the environment in a meaningful way.
Examiner: You said the garden helps you before exams. Do you think educational institutions should design their campuses specifically to support student mental health?
Candidate: Yes, I think universities have a responsibility to provide spaces that reduce stress. A classroom is good for studying, but it is not good for resting the brain. If a campus has more quiet corners and green areas, students can recharge more effectively. This design choice shows that the institution cares about the well-being of its students, not just their academic results.

Examiner: What time do you usually wake up on weekdays?
Candidate: I usually wake up at around six thirty in the morning, because I think that is the best time to get ready for my classes, and I try to be there before eight. Sometimes I feel I could wake up earlier, but I don't think it's necessary.
Examiner: Do you prefer starting your day with exercise or a meal?
Candidate: I prefer to start with a light exercise, like a short jog or some stretching, because it makes me feel more energetic than just eating breakfast. I think a jog is healthier than a big meal, and it also helps my mind to focus better during the day.
Examiner: How do you typically spend your lunch break at work or school?
Candidate: During lunch I usually go to the campus cafeteria and have a bowl of pho, then I might read a book or check my phone for messages. I try to relax a little, because I think it is the most important part of the day to recharge before the afternoon classes.
Examiner: Do you often change your daily schedule when the weekend arrives?
Candidate: On weekends I change my schedule quite a bit; I usually sleep later, maybe till nine, and I might go out with friends or do some hobby like painting. I think weekends are more flexible than weekdays, so I don't have to follow the same strict routine.
Examiner: Which social media platform do you check most frequently?
Candidate: I definitely check TikTok more than any other app because the algorithm is quite addictive. Even though I should limit my usage, I often end up scrolling for hours. The videos are shorter than others, which makes it easier to binge-watch during my lunch break without feeling too guilty about wasting time.
Examiner: Do you prefer listening to music or podcasts during your commute?
Candidate: I usually prefer music over podcasts because they are more relaxing. I can focus on my thoughts while listening to lyrics. However, I must admit that educational podcasts can be very informative, but I can not concentrate on complex topics when I am tired from studying at school all day long.
Examiner: How much screen time do you typically have on a weekday?
Candidate: Probably about six hours on average. My parents think this is the worst habit I have, but I need to use my phone for online classes and socializing. Sometimes I feel I should have less time on screens, yet I inevitably open my devices right after waking up to check for messages from friends.
Examiner: Have you ever stopped using an app you previously loved?
Candidate: Yes, I quit Instagram two months ago. I found it more stressful than helpful because I always compared my life with influencers. I could not enjoy my own hobbies anymore when I was looking at perfect photos. Now I feel much better and I manage my time much more effectively than before.
Examiner: Describe your first day at university. You should say: your expectations; the people you met; the activities you did; and explain how this experience influenced your confidence.
Candidate: I still remember my first day at university very clearly because it was a mix of excitement and nervousness that I had never felt before. I had imagined the campus would be huge and the classes would be more interesting than any high school subject, so I expected to meet a lot of friendly people and to learn a lot of new things very quickly. When I arrived early in the morning, the big stone building with the blue glass windows looked even more impressive than the pictures on the brochure, and I felt a little bit lost among the crowd of students. I met a senior named Linh who was from the same hometown as me, and she introduced me to a group of freshmen who were also looking for friends. We chatted about our subjects, and I discovered that most of them were studying engineering like me, which made me feel less alone. After the orientation lecture, we were taken on a campus tour where we visited the library, the sports complex and the cafeteria. I was most nervous than I had expected during the tour because I was afraid I would get lost, but the guide was very helpful and the group was supportive. Later, we had a short ice‑breaker activity where we had to share one interesting fact about ourselves, and I said that I could play the guitar, which surprised some of the others. By the end of the day I felt that I should could manage my schedule better and that I would be able to adapt to university life. This whole experience boosted my confidence a lot; I left the campus feeling more confident than I ever felt before, and it gave me the courage to join clubs and take part in class discussions from the very next week.
Examiner: How do you think your first day at university compares to the expectations you had before you arrived?
Candidate: I think my first day was more overwhelming than I had imagined, because the campus was larger and the crowds were louder than I expected. I believed it would be a bit easier to find my classes, but actually I got lost a couple of times, which made me feel more nervous than I thought I would be. Nevertheless, meeting Linh and the other freshmen helped me feel less isolated, and I realised that the reality could be more challenging but also more rewarding.
Examiner: You mentioned feeling nervous during the campus tour; what strategies do you think could help new students cope with such feelings?
Candidate: I would suggest that new students try to join a guided group early, because it is usually more comforting than wandering alone. Also, preparing a simple map or using a phone app might be more useful than relying only on memory. I think they should also talk to senior students like Linh, who can give advice and share experiences, which could make them feel more confident than they might feel initially. Finally, taking short breaks to breathe could calm their nerves better.
Examiner: You talked about the ice‑breaker activity; why do you believe sharing personal interests can be beneficial in a university setting?
Candidate: Sharing personal interests, like my guitar playing, can create a stronger connection among students, which is often more effective than just talking about academic subjects. It helps people see each other as individuals, not just classmates, and it can lead to collaborations in clubs or projects. I think it also makes the environment feel more inclusive than a purely lecture‑based atmosphere, and it encourages students to support each other’s hobbies, which can improve overall morale.
Examiner: Considering your schedule, how important do you think balancing academic work and extracurricular activities is for university life?
Candidate: Balancing academic work and extracurricular activities is crucial, because focusing only on studies can become more stressful than beneficial. I try to allocate time for clubs and exercise, which I think is healthier than spending all my time in the library. It also helps me manage my energy levels better, so I can stay productive during lectures. In my opinion, a well‑rounded routine can make the university experience more fulfilling than just chasing grades.
Examiner: You mentioned feeling more confident after your first day; how do you think this confidence might influence your future academic choices?
Candidate: Having that confidence makes me more likely to take on challenging courses, which I think is better than staying in my comfort zone. It also encourages me to join research groups and present my ideas, something I might have avoided before. I believe that this self‑assurance could lead me to explore interdisciplinary projects, which could be more rewarding than focusing on a single field. Ultimately, it pushes me to aim higher in my academic career.

input.text:
Examiner: What time do you usually wake up on weekdays?
Candidate: I usually get up at six-thirty. I find it very refreshing to have a head start before the city wakes up. I stretch a bit and check my schedule, so I am never in a rush to get ready for the office.
Examiner: Do you prefer starting your day with exercise or a meal?
Candidate: I strongly prefer a meal. If I exercise first, I feel dizzy and cannot focus. I like to have a light breakfast on my desk while reading news. It helps me to be alert before I start my work duties for the day.
Examiner: How do you typically spend your lunch break at work or school?
Candidate: I usually take a walk in the nearby park. The fresh air is good for my brain. If I stay inside, I feel trapped. So I spend twenty minutes outside, then I have my meal. It is a short but effective way to recharge my energy.
Examiner: Which part of your routine takes the most time each day?
Candidate: The commute is definitely the longest part. I spend almost two hours on public transport every day. It is quite tiring, but I use that time to listen to podcasts or review my notes for upcoming projects at work.
Examiner: Do you prefer reading printed books or digital versions?
Candidate: I think I prefer printed books because I like the feeling of turning pages, and I feel more focused on the story, but sometimes I also use my tablet for travel, especially when I have limited space for books in my bag, so I use both depending on the situation.
Examiner: What type of stories or articles do you enjoy reading most?
Candidate: I enjoy reading mystery novels the most, because they keep me guessing and I love trying to solve the puzzle before the ending. I also read some science articles for keeping up with new technology, especially about artificial intelligence, and sometimes I read historical fiction that transports me to another time period.
Examiner: When did you last read a book for fun?
Candidate: The last time I read a book for fun was last weekend, I finished a thriller by a Vietnamese author, and I read it on the couch in my living room, it was really exciting and I couldn't put it down until I finished the whole chapter before midnight.
Examiner: Do you read more during holidays or during the school year?
Candidate: I read more during holidays because I have more free time, but I also try to keep a habit during the school year, especially in the evenings after classes, so I can balance both study and leisure reading, which helps me relax and improve my English skills.
Examiner: Describe a memorable meal you have had. You should say: where you ate; who was with you; what made it special; and explain why it left a lasting impression on you.
Candidate: I would like to talk about a memorable meal that I had a few years ago when I visited Da Nang with my close friend Linh. We chose a small seaside restaurant that was famous for its fresh seafood, and it was located right on the beach, so we could hear the waves while we ate. The place was simple, with wooden tables and lanterns, but the view of the sunset over the ocean made it feel really special. Linh and I were the only ones at our table, and the owner, Mr. Hoang, came over to recommend the chef’s special – a grilled pomfret served with a tangy tamarind sauce, a bowl of fragrant rice and a side of pickled vegetables. The fish was cooked perfectly, the skin was crisp and the flesh was moist, and the sauce gave it a sweet‑sour flavor that I had never tasted before. While we were eating, a local musician started playing a soft guitar melody, and the whole atmosphere turned into a kind of quiet celebration. What made the meal stand out was not just the food but also the sense of connection I felt with Linh, because we were sharing stories about our families and future plans, and the sea breeze seemed to carry our laughter. If I think back to that night, I can still remember the taste of the tamarind sauce and the feeling of the warm sand under our feet after we walked along the shore. It left a lasting impression because it combined great food, beautiful scenery and a moment of genuine friendship that I still cherish whenever I think about travelling.
Examiner: You mentioned that the atmosphere turned into a quiet celebration. Do you think music significantly changes how people experience a meal?
Candidate: Yes, I strongly believe that it does. When background music is playing, the dining experience becomes more than just eating; it transforms into a social event. People tend to speak softer and enjoy the moment more. In my view, if there is no music, the place feels a bit sterile, especially in restaurants that aim for a romantic or relaxed vibe. The sound sets the mood for the entire evening.
Examiner: You noted that the view of the sunset made it feel special. Is the location more important than the food itself for a memorable meal?
Candidate: It depends on who you ask, but I think location plays a huge role. A mediocre dish can taste amazing if you are sitting by a beach or a river. Conversely, if the place is noisy or dirty, even the best chef cannot save the meal. The visual and sensory environment creates memories, so the setting is often more memorable than the taste on the tongue, I would say.
Examiner: You talked about sharing stories with your friend Linh. How has the way people share meals with friends changed in recent years?
Candidate: I think it has become more fragmented. In the past, everyone would sit at one big table and talk. Now, people often have their phones in front of them. I feel like we are physically together but mentally in our own worlds. It is a bit sad because the conversation is not as deep as it used to be, and we miss out on the real connection that happens over food.
Examiner: You mentioned the tangy tamarind sauce. Do you think traditional local ingredients are disappearing from modern restaurants?
Candidate: To some extent, yes. Many new restaurants try to be trendy and use imported ingredients or fusion styles. Younger chefs might not know how to cook traditional dishes properly. However, I am hopeful because there is a growing movement to preserve culinary heritage. If these old recipes are not taught to the next generation, we will lose the unique flavors that define our culture.
Examiner: You said you can still remember the taste of that night. Why do food memories tend to last longer than other types of experiences?
Candidate: I think it is because food is linked to emotion and comfort. When you taste something delicious, your brain releases happy chemicals. Also, food is often shared with loved ones, so the memory is tied to the people present, not just the meal itself. A bad day can be fixed with a good meal, so the association is very strong and hard to forget, unlike a simple conversation.

input.text:
Examiner: What time do you usually wake up on weekdays?
Candidate: Usually I wake up at around six thirty in the morning, because I have to catch the bus to school and I like to have a little time to review my notes before the first class starts.
Examiner: Do you prefer starting your day with exercise or a meal?
Candidate: I think I prefer having a meal first, especially a simple breakfast like rice porridge and some fruit, because if I exercise right after waking up I feel a bit dizzy, so I usually eat and then I might do a short walk if the weather is nice.
Examiner: What is the last thing you do before going to bed?
Candidate: The last thing I do is usually check my phone for any messages from my friends or family, and then I set my alarm, I brush my teeth and I read a few pages of a novel until I feel sleepy.
Examiner: Do you often change your daily schedule when the weekend arrives?
Candidate: On weekends I often change my schedule a bit, I might sleep later and I would meet my friends for coffee, sometimes I go to the market or help my parents at home, but I still try to keep a short study session so I don't fall behind.
Examiner: What type of stories or articles do you enjoy reading most?
Candidate: I usually prefer mystery novels because they keep me on the edge of my seat. If the plot is too predictable, I find it hard to stay engaged. I also read a lot of news articles to stay updated on global events, which helps me broaden my perspective on current affairs.
Examiner: When did you last read a book for fun?
Candidate: I started reading a sci-fi novel last weekend, but I did not finish it yet. I only read a few chapters because I was quite busy with my school exams. I plan to continue it next week when I have more free time.
Examiner: Do you read more during holidays or during the school year?
Candidate: Definitely during the holidays. If the school year is on, I have so much homework that I barely have any time for personal reading. During breaks, I can spend hours in the library or just sitting in my room reading without feeling rushed.
Examiner: Do you ever recommend books to your friends or family?
Candidate: Yes, I often share books that I think are interesting with my close friends. I did recommend a poetry collection to my sister last month, and she seemed to enjoy it quite a bit. It is nice to share things that bring us joy.
Examiner: Describe a challenging project you worked on. You should say: the goal of the project; the obstacles you faced; the outcome; and explain how you felt after completing it.
Candidate: I’d like to talk about a challenging project I worked on during my final year of high school, it was a science fair exhibition where our team had to design a simple water purification system using locally available materials. The main goal of the project was to create a device that could reduce contaminants in river water to a level safe for drinking, and we also wanted to present the whole process in a clear and engaging way for the judges and other students. At first, I thought it would be easy because we had some basic knowledge about filtration, but soon we faced several obstacles. One big problem was that the budget was very limited, so we could not buy commercial filters and we had to improvise with sand, charcoal and some plastic bottles. Another difficulty was that the chemistry teacher, who was supposed to guide us, was away for a few weeks, so we had to figure out the right chemical reactions on our own. If I would have known how important the teacher’s input was, I might have planned a backup plan earlier. Also, we ran into time constraints because the school schedule changed and we lost a week of lab access, which meant we had to work late evenings at home. During the testing phase, the prototype kept leaking, and I think we tried different sealing methods but none of them worked at first. Eventually, we discovered that using a rubber gasket from an old bike tire solved the leakage problem. The outcome was that we managed to produce a functional purifier that could lower turbidity by about seventy percent, and we won the second prize at the fair. After the presentation, I felt a mixture of relief and pride. I was relieved because all the hard work finally paid off, and I was proud because I learned how to solve problems creatively and work as a team under pressure. Looking back, the experience also taught me that planning for unexpected issues and asking for help early can make a big difference in any project.
Examiner: You mentioned that your team had to improvise with limited resources. Do you think schools should provide more funding for such practical projects?
Candidate: I believe that having adequate funding is crucial for students to explore their ideas fully. If schools had more budget, they might buy better equipment, which could lead to more sophisticated results. However, I also think that working with limited resources teaches us valuable lessons about creativity and adaptability. It forces us to think outside the box. So, while money is helpful, it should not be the only tool we rely on. We need to balance financial support with the challenge of solving problems using what we have.
Examiner: You said the absence of your chemistry teacher was a significant obstacle. How do you think reliance on a single expert can affect a team's ability to innovate?
Candidate: It can be quite limiting. If a team depends too much on one person, they might not develop their own critical thinking skills. In my case, we had to figure out the chemical reactions on our own, which was difficult but also empowering. It showed us that we had the capability to find answers independently. However, if the problem was too complex, we might have failed. So, having access to diverse expertise is beneficial, but it should encourage collaboration rather than passive waiting for instructions.
Examiner: You mentioned that the school schedule change caused time constraints. Do you think modern education systems place too much emphasis on theory at the expense of hands-on experience?
Candidate: Yes, I often feel that way. Many students spend years memorizing facts, but they do not have enough time to apply those facts in real-world scenarios. When we lost lab access, it highlighted how fragile our practical skills were. If students engage more with hands-on projects, they might understand concepts better. For example, building a purifier helps you understand filtration far more than reading about it. Schools should try to integrate more practical work into the regular curriculum to prepare students for real life.
Examiner: You felt a mixture of relief and pride after winning the prize. How important is it for young people to experience success in collaborative tasks before entering the workforce?
Candidate: It is extremely important. Experiencing success in a team environment builds confidence and teaches us how to communicate effectively. When we won the second prize, it was not just about the trophy; it was about the process. We learned how to handle pressure and how to support each other. If young people only experience failure or work alone, they might struggle with team dynamics later. Early success can motivate them to take on bigger challenges and develop the interpersonal skills that are essential in almost every career.
Examiner: You noted that you learned to solve problems creatively under pressure. Do you think this kind of resilience can be taught, or is it a natural trait?
Candidate: I think it can be taught to some extent. While some people might be naturally more adaptable, resilience is a skill that improves with practice. If students are given opportunities to face difficult situations in a safe environment, they can learn how to cope. My experience with the leaking prototype taught me that problems are not necessarily failures. They are just steps in the process. By encouraging students to reflect on their challenges and how they overcame them, educators can help them build this resilience. It becomes a habit over time.

It shows you have considered their taste and you put effort into choosing something that fits their lifestyle.
Examiner: Would you prefer a cash gift or a physical object?
Candidate: Honestly, I would rather receive a physical object because it can stay with me and bring memories. Cash is useful, but it feels a bit impersonal, like just a number on a piece of paper. A well‑chosen item can tell a story and make the moment more memorable.
Examiner: When is the best time of year to buy presents for family?
Candidate: I think the best time to buy gifts for family is at the beginning of the holiday season, around November, because stores have many discounts and you have enough time to wrap them nicely. Also, buying early avoids the last‑minute rush and gives you a chance to think carefully about each present.
Examiner: What is the most popular meal you prepare at home?
Candidate: I think it is stir-fried vegetables with eggs, because it is very fast to cook on busy workdays. My family loves this dish and I am quite confident in making it tasty. Sometimes I add a little bit of chili to make it have more flavor, which I find quite exciting.
Examiner: Have you tried cooking a dish from a different country recently?
Candidate: Yes, a couple of weeks ago I watched a video tutorial and decided to attempt pasta. It was a bit challenging for me, but I am quite proud that I finished it. The texture was not exactly like in restaurants, but the taste was quite acceptable and I felt very happy about it.
Examiner: What food item do you avoid eating and why?
Candidate: I really do not like eating durian, because the smell is too strong and it makes me feel a little bit sick on my stomach. I think it is not a pleasant experience for me to have it, so I usually just avoid it completely whenever I go out to eat with friends.
Examiner: Which cuisine would you like to learn to cook next?
Candidate: I am quite interested in learning Japanese cuisine, especially sushi and sashimi. I think the presentation is very beautiful and the ingredients are fresh, which I find very appealing. I want to try making it at home to impress my friends during our next dinner party, so it is on my list.
Examiner: Describe a favorite seasonal festival you celebrate. You should say: the time of year; the traditions involved; the people you celebrate with; and explain what the festival means to you.
Candidate: Well, I would like to talk about the Lunar New Year festival, which is my favourite seasonal celebration every year. It usually falls in late January or early February, so it is a winter festival for us, although the weather is starting to get warmer. The most important tradition is the family reunion dinner, which we have on the eve of the new year at home. We clean the house completely before that day, because it is believed that cleaning removes the bad luck from the previous year. Then we decorate the living room with red lanterns and couplets, and we put a special cake on the table for the ancestors. Another tradition is the giving of lucky money, called "li xi", which we give to children and also to younger relatives, and we do it in the morning after the first sunrise of the new year. We also go to the temple for a prayer, where we light incense and offer fruits on the altar, and we stay there for about half an hour. I usually celebrate with my parents, my wife and my two children, and sometimes my older brother comes from the city to join us. My friends also come over to share some traditional foods, such as spring rolls and sticky rice cakes. The festival means a lot to me because it is not only about having fun, it is about respecting our culture and keeping the family bond strong. It reminds me of my childhood when I used to watch my grandparents preparing the food and telling stories about the ancient customs. In a way, celebrating Lunar New Year each year gives me a sense of continuity and hope for the future, and it also helps me to stay connected with my roots while living in a modern city.
Examiner: How do you think seasonal festivals like the Lunar New Year influence people’s sense of cultural identity?
Candidate: I believe that festivals such as the Lunar New Year have a strong impact on cultural identity because they bring people together in shared rituals. When we gather for the reunion dinner, we are not only eating food but also practising traditions that have been passed down for generations. This kind of participation creates a feeling of belonging and pride, especially for younger members who might otherwise feel detached from their roots. Even though we live in a modern city, the festival acts like a bridge between the old customs and our everyday life, reinforcing who we are as a community.
Examiner: You mentioned the importance of family reunion dinner. In what ways can such gatherings affect family relationships over time?
Candidate: The family reunion dinner can strengthen relationships because it provides a regular occasion for members to interact face‑to‑face, which is something that is often missing in our busy lives. When we sit together at the table, we share stories, laugh, and sometimes even resolve old misunderstandings in a more relaxed atmosphere. This repeated contact builds trust and emotional bonds, especially between parents and children. Moreover, the act of preparing the meal together, like cooking spring rolls or sticky rice cakes, creates shared memories that act as a reminder of our unity during the whole year.
Examiner: You talked about cleaning the house before the festival. What significance does this practice hold in the broader context of society?
Candidate: Cleaning the house before the new year is symbolic; it is believed to sweep away the bad luck from the previous year, which reflects a desire for a fresh start in society. On a larger scale, when whole neighborhoods engage in this activity, it promotes a collective sense of renewal and optimism. It also encourages people to be more mindful about their surroundings, fostering communal responsibility. This ritual can even influence social behavior, as individuals might feel more inclined to start new projects or improve relationships after the symbolic cleaning.
Examiner: Considering the giving of lucky money, how do you think monetary gifts affect the dynamics between generations?
Candidate: Lucky money, or "li xi", plays an interesting role in intergenerational dynamics because it combines material support with cultural symbolism. For younger relatives, receiving money can be a source of encouragement and a reminder of the elder’s care, which may strengthen respect towards older family members. Conversely, elders who give the money often feel a sense of responsibility and fulfillment, as they are contributing to the younger generation’s future. However, there can be a risk that the focus shifts more to the amount rather than the gesture, which might affect the authenticity of the relationship if not balanced properly.
Examiner: Do you think modern technology has changed the way people celebrate traditional festivals? If so, how?
Candidate: Modern technology definitely changes the celebration of traditional festivals. For instance, many families now use video calls to include relatives who live far away, allowing them to join the reunion dinner virtually, which was impossible a few decades ago. Social media also spreads images of decorations and recipes, encouraging people to adopt new ideas while keeping the core customs. On the other hand, the reliance on digital gifts, like e‑cards or electronic lucky money, can dilute the personal touch that physical gifts provide. Overall, technology expands participation but also challenges us to keep the authentic spirit of the festival alive.

input.text:
Examiner: Do you prefer reading printed books or digital versions?
Candidate: To be honest, I have a strong preference for physical books. There is something quite tactile about turning the pages and feeling the weight of the volume in my hands that simply cannot be replicated on a screen. Digital formats are certainly more convenient for travel, but I find that I focus better when I am not constantly distracted by notifications popping up on my phone.
Examiner: What type of stories or articles do you enjoy reading most?
Candidate: I tend to gravitate towards literary fiction and non-fiction pieces about psychology. I find it fascinating to explore the complexities of human behavior and see how different authors interpret social dynamics. Lately, I have been really into biographies of successful entrepreneurs because they often contain practical insights that I can apply to my own career development and daily life situations.
Examiner: When did you last read a book for fun?
Candidate: It was actually just a few days ago. I spent a rainy Sunday afternoon finishing a novel called The Silent Echo. It was a really engaging story about a family dealing with a mysterious inheritance. I barely noticed the time flying by, which is a great sign. I usually only get around to reading for pleasure when I have a bit of free time.
Examiner: Do you read more during holidays or during the school year?
Candidate: Definitely during holidays. When I am working full-time, my evenings are usually consumed by rest and social commitments, so I rarely have the mental energy to sit down with a new book. However, during vacation, I can dedicate entire mornings to reading without feeling rushed. It is one of the few times of year when I can truly disconnect from my work responsibilities.
Examiner: Which social media platform do you check most frequently?
Candidate: I think it's Instagram, because I use it for both staying in touch with friends and following news. I usually open it first thing in the morning, and then again during lunch break, so I end up checking it maybe five or six times a day, especially when there are new stories or live videos.
Examiner: How much screen time do you typically have on a weekday?
Candidate: On a typical weekday I would say I spend around three to four hours in front of screen, including work, social media and some videos. I try to limit it after work, but sometimes I end up watching series on Netflix because I want to relax, so total can reach close to five hours sometimes.
Examiner: What type of video game would you enjoy playing for fun?
Candidate: I really enjoy playing role‑playing games, especially ones with open worlds where I can explore and complete quests. I like the freedom to make choices, and the stories are usually very engaging. When I have free time I often pick up a game like "Elder Scrolls" because it lets me get lost in fantasy setting for hours.
Examiner: Have you ever stopped using an app you previously loved?
Candidate: Yes, I actually stopped using a photo‑editing app that I loved a lot. It was great for adding filters, but after a while the updates became too frequent and it started using a lot of battery, so I decided to switch to another one that is more stable and doesn't require so many permissions.
Examiner: Describe a gift that you received which you still treasure. You should say: who gave it to you; what the item looks like; when you received it; and explain why it remains so important to you.
Candidate: I’d like to talk about a gift that I received a few years ago and still keep it close to my heart. It was given to me by my older sister, Linh, on the day I graduated from university. She handed me a small wooden box, about the size of a paperback book, with intricate carvings of lotus flowers and swirling patterns on its lid. Inside, there was a leather‑bound journal, its pages slightly yellowed, and a silver pen that felt surprisingly heavy when I held it. I remember the moment vividly because the ceremony was held in a quiet garden, and after everyone had taken photos, Linh pulled me aside and said, "I hope you write down all your dreams in this," with a smile that made me feel both proud and a little nervous about future.

What makes this gift so special isn’t just its appearance but the meaning behind it. The wooden box itself is handcrafted by a local artisan in my hometown, and each time I look at the lotus carvings, I think of my family’s roots and the calmness that lotus represents in Vietnamese culture. The journal, on the other hand, became a place where I recorded my first job experiences, travel plans, and even some poetry I wrote during late nights. Even though I’ve moved to a new city for work, I still keep the box on my desk, and the pen sits right next to my laptop, reminding me of the support that Linh gave me.

It remains important because it symbolizes a turning point in my life – the transition from student to professional – and it carries the love and encouragement of my sister. Whenever I feel stressed or uncertain, I open the journal, read the first entry I wrote on graduation day, and it instantly lifts my spirits, making me feel connected to my past and motivated for future challenges.
Examiner: You mentioned that the wooden box is handcrafted by a local artisan. Do you think traditional crafts are at risk of disappearing in modern cities?
Candidate: I believe that there is a genuine risk, but it is not inevitable. In many big cities, people are increasingly turned towards mass-produced goods that are cheaper and more accessible. However, I have noticed a growing appreciation for unique, handmade items among younger generations who value authenticity over convenience. If we continue to support local artisans and educate the public on the cultural significance behind these objects, we can ensure that these skills are passed down to next generation. It is about creating a balance between economic efficiency and preserving our heritage.
Examiner: You said you record your first job experiences in the journal. How has technology changed the way people document their personal histories?
Candidate: Technology has definitely made documenting life easier, but perhaps less intimate. Most people now rely on social media posts or digital photo albums, which are often fleeting and public. Unlike a private journal, these digital records are easily searchable but also easily deleted. I think that there is a lack of depth in modern documentation because we often capture moments for others rather than for ourselves. A handwritten entry requires reflection and slows down the process, which forces us to think more critically about our experiences and emotions.
Examiner: You mentioned that the lotus represents calmness in Vietnamese culture. Why do you think symbols like this remain so powerful in a globalized world?
Candidate: I think that symbols like the lotus remain powerful because they provide a sense of identity and belonging, which is crucial in a fast-paced, globalized society. When we look at these traditional symbols, they serve as a reminder of our roots and values, helping us to stay grounded amidst constant change. They are universal in their meaning of purity and resilience, but they are deeply personal to those who share that culture. This combination of universal and personal meaning gives them a lasting emotional resonance that abstract concepts often lack.
Examiner: You noted that the gift symbolizes the transition from student to professional. Do you think societies place too much pressure on young people to achieve this transition quickly?
Candidate: Yes, I do think there is an excessive amount of pressure. Many young people feel that they need to secure a high-paying job and buy a house immediately after graduation to prove their worth. This rush can lead to burnout and poor decision-making, as they may choose careers for prestige rather than passion. In my opinion, society should value the process of personal growth as much as professional milestones. It is important to allow individuals to explore different paths and find their own pace, rather than forcing them into a rigid timeline of success.
Examiner: You said that reading the first entry lifts your spirits. How do you think physical objects can influence a person's emotional state more effectively than digital reminders?
Candidate: Physical objects have a tangible presence that digital reminders simply cannot replicate. When I hold that silver pen, I can feel its weight and texture, which creates a multisensory connection to the past. A digital notification is transient and easy to ignore, but a physical object sits in your personal space, constantly reminding you of a specific memory. This tactile interaction grounds you in the present moment while linking you to your emotional history. It is a more deliberate and focused way to reconnect with one's inner self and memories.
